B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

B001317.text: This week, @freedomcaucus delivered for the American people. The Senate must continue the House’s momentum and pass Reconciliation 3.0 and the SAVE America Act immediately!

Today, I voted “no” on the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal year 2027. While I support providing for a robust national defense, I could not in good conscience vote for this legislation as it authorizes a $263.4 billion (29.6%) increase over the authorized level for the previous fiscal year. Looking to history, we know that once a level of spending is authorized, appropriators will rarely provide less funding than the maximum allowed. Furthermore, departmental funding baselines almost never decrease over time. Our Founding Fathers believed that public debt was among “the greatest of the dangers to be feared.” As George Washington once wrote, “avoiding likewise the accumulation of debt, not only by shunning occasions of expense, but by vigorous exertions in time of peace to discharge the debts, which unavoidable wars may have occasioned, not ungenerously throwing upon posterity the burthen, which we ourselves ought to bear.” We are currently facing the largest national debt in our country’s history, owing over $39.5 trillion, and we simply cannot bear the cost of additional, unpaid-for spending. To achieve the transformative defense spending necessary for our nation’s future, we must either, in the current Reconciliation 3.0 or in a future reconciliation package, find meaningful offsets that would allow us to reach a higher annual defense spending target in a fiscally responsible way. Unlike providing additional defense funding in a reconciliation package, which is a one-time expenditure, this bill would be a $260 billion increase in the annual defense discretionary baseline that I could support if we offset the cost elsewhere. Without any further changes to spending, this would mean roughly $2.63 trillion in additional debt loading over the next ten years. While I cannot support this package due to my spending concerns, I support the SAVE America Act being joined to this legislation after final passage. I have voted in favor of the SAVE America Act and its predecessor, the SAVE Act, five times. I support leadership’s decision to join the SAVE America Act to other pieces of legislation whenever they can, but I cannot vote for legislation that could lead to an additional debt load of $2.63 trillion over the next ten years. I continue to be hopeful that we will be able to pass the SAVE America Act through the reconciliation process, which we advanced this week.

Thank you, Mr. President! As fiscal hawks in the House, we have put aside our spending offset demands in this measure SOLELY because of the expectation that this is the path for the Senate to pass the SAVE America Act in truth…not a ‘dead on arrival’ counterfeit version some in the Senate are advocating.

M001228.text: RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

Today, we mourn the passing of United States Senator Lindsey Graham, a fierce advocate for the people of South Carolina.  May his memory be a blessing to his family and friends. Lindsey’s unexpected passing also affirms a profound truth: every day we live is a gift and a blessing from God.

Il y a dix ans aujourd’hui, il était lâchement assassiné par deux terroristes islamistes, pris pour cible parce qu’il incarnait le refus de la haine, la fraternité et l’espérance. À ses proches, à ses paroissiens et à tous les habitants de Saint-Étienne-du-Rouvray, aux catholiques de France, j’adresse le salut fraternel et fidèle de la Nation. Sa mémoire nous oblige. Elle nous oblige à défendre sans relâche la liberté de conscience que garantit et protège la République. Face au terrorisme islamiste, la France reste unie. Fidèle à ce qui la fonde. Résolue à ne rien céder à ceux qui veulent nous diviser.
